For God, being by nature good and kind, has a special occasion of showing mercy and giving help to the poor and to persons in misery. Therefore it is written in Deuteronomy: The Lord [[Deut 10:18|doth judgment to the fatherless and the widow, loveth the stranger|facit judicium pupillo et viduæ, amatque peregrinum]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 145:7|who executeth judgment for them that suffer wrong|Facit judicium injuriam patientibus]]; [[Ps 145:9|The Lord keepeth the strangers, he will support the fatherless and the widow|Dominus custodit advenas, pupillum et viduam suscipiet]].

paras.t: Hinc Christus in exordio suæ prædicationis pauperes piscatores ad discipulatum suum vocavit : qui et in Luca testatur, Beati pauperes, quoniam vestrum est regnum Dei. Pauperibus namque ipsa eorum paupertas quotidianum purgatorium invenitur. Elegit itaque Deus pauperes, quos ab æterno elegit, et suo tempore per gratiam suam vocavit. Unde subjungitur : divites in fide : non quod ante electionem et vocationem fuerint spiritualiter divites in fide, sed ex sua electione et pietate fecit eos spiritualiter opulentos per fidem et cetera gratiarum charismata fidei annexa. Veræ quippe divitiæ sunt virtutes ac meritoria opera. Unde in prima ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus : Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe, divites fieri in operibus bonis. Et quia tales electi, sunt ad futuram beatitudinem prædestinati, de eis subjungitur : et heredes regni quod repromisit Deus diligentibus se. De quibus ait Apostolus : Scimus quoniam diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum, his qui secundum propositum vocati sunt sancti. Quidam enim diligunt Deum ad tempus, sed non perseverant in caritate finaliter; quos constat prædestinatos non esse. Hinc loquitur Christus : Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum.
paras.en: Hence Christ, at the beginning of his preaching, called poor fishermen to be his disciples; and in Luke he declares: [[Luke 6:20|Blessed are ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God|Beati pauperes, quoniam vestrum est regnum Dei]]. For the poor find in their very poverty a daily purgatory. So God has chosen the poor, whom he chose from eternity and called in his own time by his grace. Hence it is added: [[2:5|rich in faith|divites in fide]]: not that before their election and calling they were spiritually rich in faith, but by his election and kindness he made them spiritually wealthy through faith and the other gifts of grace joined to faith. For true riches are the virtues and meritorious works. Hence the Apostle writes in the first Epistle to Timothy: [[1 Tim 6:17|Charge the rich of this world|Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe]] [[1 Tim 6:18|to be rich in good work|divites fieri in operibus bonis]]. And because such elect are predestined to the bliss to come, it is added of them: [[2:5|and heirs of the kingdom which God hath promised to them that love him?|et heredes regni quod repromisit Deus diligentibus se]]. Of whom the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:28|we know that to them that love God all things work together unto good: to such as, according to his purpose, are called to be saints|Scimus quoniam diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum, his qui secundum propositum vocati sunt sancti]]. For some love God for a time, but do not persevere in charity to the end; and it is certain that these are not predestined. Hence Christ says: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]].

paras.t: Vos autem exhonorastis pauperem. Pauperes ergo propter charismata gratiæ eis collata, sunt honorandi, et maxime quia frequentius sunt a Deo electi. Divites vero propter suarum abusus divitiarum, et cetera scelera sua, sunt zelo justitiæ despiciendi, in quantum sunt tales, sicut de justo fertur in Psalmo : Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus; timentes autem Dominum glorificat. Unde et Salomon loquitur : Melior est pauper qui ambulat in simplicitate sua, quam dives torquens labia sua; et rursus. Melius est modicum cum timore Domini, quam thesauri multi. Propterea subditur : Nonne divites per potentiam opprimunt vos, et ipsi trahunt vos ad judicia, id est, judicibus vos præsentant tanquam reos, eo quod estis Christiani?
paras.en: [[2:6|But you have dishonoured the poor man|Vos autem exhonorastis pauperem]]. The poor, then, are to be honoured for the gifts of grace bestowed on them, and above all because they are more often chosen by God. But the rich, for their abuse of their riches and their other crimes, are to be despised with a zeal for justice, insofar as they are such; as is said of the just man in the Psalm: [[Ps 14:4|In his sight the malignant is brought to nothing: but he glorifieth them that fear the Lord|Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus; timentes autem Dominum glorificat]]. Hence Solomon too says: [[Prov 19:1|Better is the poor man, that walketh in his simplicity, than a rich man that is perverse in his lips|Melior est pauper qui ambulat in simplicitate sua, quam dives torquens labia sua]]; and again: [[Prov 15:16|Better is a little with the fear of the Lord, than great treasures|Melius est modicum cum timore Domini, quam thesauri multi]]. Therefore it is added: [[2:6|Do not the rich oppress you by might|Nonne divites per potentiam opprimunt vos]]? [[2:6|And do not they draw you before the judgment seats|et ipsi trahunt vos ad judicia]]? That is, do they not bring you before judges as guilty men, because you are Christians?

paras.t: Nonne ipsi blasphemant bonum nomen nominatum, quod invocatum est super vos, id est nomen Christi seu Christum, quem negant esse verum Messiam in lege promissum? Hæc in primitiva Ecclesia passim fecerunt divites infideles, tam Judæi quam gentiles, Christianis qui Christum jugiter invocabant, et quem pro se invicem exorabant.
paras.en: [[2:7|Do not they blaspheme the good name|Nonne ipsi blasphemant bonum nomen]] which has been named [*nominatum*, a word not in the Clementine text], [[2:7|that is invoked upon you|quod invocatum est super vos]]? That is, the name of Christ, or Christ himself, whom they deny to be the true Messias promised in the law. This the unbelieving rich, Jews and gentiles alike, did everywhere in the early Church to the Christians, who called upon Christ continually and besought him for one another.

paras.t: Si tamen legem perficitis regalem, id est legem divinam, a Rege altissimo datam, regia via incedentem, eo quod neque ad dexteram neque ad sinistram divertat, nec aliquid obliquitatis contineat. De qua in Isaia legitur : Hæc via, ambulate in ea, et neque ad dexteram neque ad sinistram declinetis; atque in Psalmo, Lex Domini immaculata. De qua et in Proverbiis asseritur : Lex lux est. Si, inquam, hanc legem perficitis, id est, perfecte impletis, secundum Scripturas, id est, prout in Scripturis sanctis docetur ac continetur. Deinde exprimit legem istam in speciali, seu quantum ad mandatum ejus præcipuum post primum ac summum legis præceptum. Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum : id est, spiritualiter desiderando ei bona gratiæ ac virtutum in via, donaque gloriæ in patria, imo et cooperando ei ad ista pro posse; cetera quoque misericordiæ opera, tam corporalia quam spiritualia, ei impertiendo pro viribus, tempore opportuno, exigente rationabili causa. Bene facitis. Quasi dicat Apostolus : Non ita dico divites pauperibus non esse præferendos, quasi sint odiendi, aut simpliciter contemnendi, quum ex divino præcepto sint diligendi. Sed eorum dilectio ordinate est exhibenda eisdem, salvo ordine æquitatis, ut non derogetur justitiæ in pauperum depressione.
paras.en: [[2:8|If then you fulfil the royal law|Si tamen legem perficitis regalem]], that is, the divine law, given by the most high King, which goes by the royal road [*regia via*, "the king's highway": a play on *regalem*, "royal"], since it turns aside neither to the right hand nor to the left, and holds nothing crooked. Of it we read in Isaias: [[Is 30:21|This is the way, walk ye in it: and go not aside neither to the right hand, nor to the left|Hæc via, ambulate in ea, et neque ad dexteram neque ad sinistram declinetis]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 18:8|The law of the Lord is unspotted|Lex Domini immaculata]]. Of it too it is affirmed in Proverbs: [[Prov 6:23|the law a light|Lex lux est]]. If, I say, you fulfil this law, that is, fulfil it perfectly, [[2:8|according to the scriptures|secundum Scripturas]], that is, as is taught and contained in the holy Scriptures. Then he sets out this law in particular, that is, as to its chief commandment after the first and greatest commandment of the law: [[2:8|Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself|Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum]][[Lev 19:18||]][[Matt 5:43||]]: that is, by desiring for him spiritually the goods of grace and of the virtues on the way, and the gifts of glory in the homeland, and indeed by working with him towards these as far as one can; and also by bestowing on him, as far as one is able, the other works of mercy, corporal as well as spiritual, at a fitting time, when a reasonable cause requires it. [[2:8|you do well|Bene facitis]]. As if the Apostle were saying: I do not say that the rich are not to be preferred to the poor as though they were to be hated or simply despised, since by God's commandment they are to be loved. But love is to be shown them in due order, saving the order of equity, so that justice is not violated by the oppression of the poor.

paras.t: Si autem personas accipitis (juxta sensum præhabitum), peccatum operamini, faciendo contra præceptum Dei. Propter quod subditur : redarguti a lege quasi transgressores divini præcepti. Et ita hæc dictio, Quasi, dicit hic veritatem, non similitudinem tantum : quemadmodum et Joannes inquit, Vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre. Ista quippe personarum acceptio, in lege Mosaica atque evangelica prohibetur : quoniam in Levitico Dominus ait, Juste judicabis, nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis. In Deuteronomio quoque Moyses ait principibus et judicibus Israel : Audite illos, et quod justum est, judicate, sive civis ille sit, sive peregrinus : nulla erit distantia; ita parvum audietis ut magnum, nec accipietis cujusquam personam. Christus etiam jubet : Nolite judicare secundum faciem, sed justum judicium judicate. Hinc in libro Job Eliu contestatur : Non accipiam personam viri. Debemus ergo non personas, sed causas accipere.
paras.en: [[2:9|But if you have respect to persons|Si autem personas accipitis]] (in the sense given above), [[2:9|you commit sin|peccatum operamini]], by acting against the commandment of God. Because of which it is added: [[2:9|being reproved by the law as transgressors|redarguti a lege quasi transgressores]] of the divine commandment. And so this word *as* [*quasi*, which can also mean "as it were"] expresses the truth here, not merely a likeness: just as John too says: [[John 1:14|we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father|Vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre]]. For this respect of persons is forbidden in the law of Moses and in the law of the Gospel: since in Leviticus the Lord says: Thou shalt judge justly; [[Lev 19:15|Respect not the person of the poor: nor honour the countenance of the mighty|nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis]]. In Deuteronomy too Moses says to the princes and judges of Israel: [[Deut 1:16|Hear them, and judge that which is just: whether he be one of your country, or a stranger|Audite illos, et quod justum est, judicate, sive civis ille sit, sive peregrinus]]: [[Deut 1:17|There shall be no difference of persons, you shall hear the little as well as the great: neither shall you respect any man's person|nulla erit distantia; ita parvum audietis ut magnum, nec accipietis cujusquam personam]]. Christ also commands: [[John 7:24|Judge not according to the appearance: but judge just judgment|Nolite judicare secundum faciem, sed justum judicium judicate]]. Hence in the book of Job Eliu protests: [[Job 32:21|I will not accept the person of man|Non accipiam personam viri]]. We ought, then, to have regard not to persons but to causes.

paras.t: Circa prædicta, ut clarius intelligantur, aliqua sunt quærenda : primo, an personarum acceptio sit peccatum mortale ; secundo, in quibus committatur hoc vitium ; tertio, an Deo conveniat personarum acceptio.
paras.en: Concerning what has been said, so that it may be more clearly understood, some questions must be asked: first, whether respect of persons is a mortal sin; second, in what things this vice is committed; third, whether respect of persons befits God.

paras.t: Quantum ad primum, videtur ex præinductis Jacobi verbis, ceterisque auctoritatibus allegatis, quod personarum acceptio sit mortale peccatum. Quod etiam aliunde probatur : quia sicut illud est ex suo genere culpa mortalis, quod est contra caritatem, ita et id quod est contra justitiam. Sed personarum acceptio directe contrariatur distributivæ justitiæ. Verumtamen videtur oppositum : quia si divitem plus honorare quam pauperem, est mortale peccatum, omnes periclitamur, et in statu esse damnationis videmur. Quis enim non facit hoc? Quis ponit pauperem ad mensam suam, ut divitem? Quis ita salutat egenum, ut locupletem? — Ad hæc respondet Albertus : Quod si dives magis honoretur quam pauper, per respectum et promotionem ad ecclesiasticas dignitates ad quas fuerit indignus, mortale est vitium : ut si dives, sapientia et virtutibus carens, ad ecclesiasticos promoveatur honores, pauper vero abjiciatur, qui sapientia, vita et moribus promotione tali est dignus. Hinc Beda allegat Augustinum, dicentem : Si hanc distantiam sedendi et standi, de qua Jacobus loquitur, ad honores ecclesiasticos referamus, non est putandum leve esse peccatum, in personarum acceptione habere fidem Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Quis enim ferat eligi divitem ad sedem honoris Ecclesiæ, contempto paupere instructiore ac sanctiore?
paras.en: As to the first: it seems, from the words of James brought forward above and the other authorities cited, that respect of persons is a mortal sin. This is also proved from another quarter: for just as whatever is against charity is a mortal fault of its kind, so too is whatever is against justice. But respect of persons is directly contrary to distributive justice. And yet the opposite seems to be the case: for if it is a mortal sin to honour the rich man more than the poor, we are all in peril and seem to be in a state of damnation. For who does not do this? Who sets a poor man at his table as he does a rich one? Who greets a needy man as he does a wealthy one? To this Albert replies that if the rich man is honoured more than the poor by regard for him and promotion to ecclesiastical dignities of which he is unworthy, it is a mortal vice: as if a rich man lacking wisdom and virtue were promoted to ecclesiastical honours, and a poor man cast aside who by his wisdom, life and conduct is worthy of such promotion. Hence Bede cites Augustine, who says: If we refer this difference of sitting and standing of which James speaks to the honours of the Church, it is not to be thought a light sin to have [[2:1|the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ|fidem Domini nostri Jesu Christi]] [[2:1|with respect of persons|in personarum acceptione]]. For who could bear that a rich man should be chosen for a seat of honour in the Church, while a poor man more learned and more holy is despised?

paras.t: Quocirca pensandum, quia ut in secunda secundæ asserit Thomas, dignitas personæ considerari potest dupliciter : Primo, simpliciter et in se : et ita qui sapientior virtuosiorque consistit, absolute est melior. Secundo, per comparationem ad bonum commune : et sic potest contingere, ut qui absolute loquendo minus bonus est, utpote minus virtuosus et doctus, sit bono communi utilior ratione potentiæ sive industriæ, aut alicujus hujusmodi. Quum igitur dispensationes spiritualium ad communem utilitatem potissimum ordinentur, idcirco interdum minus boni melioribus præferuntur in talibus absque personarum acceptione. Porro secundum jura, ad valorem electionis sufficit eligere bonum atque idoneum. Nec oportet eligere meliorem secundum forum judiciale : alias electio posset quasi semper calumniari. Sed quoad eligentis conscientiam, oportet eligere meliorem, vel simpliciter, vel per comparationem ad bonum commune.
paras.en: Here it must be considered that, as Thomas affirms in the Secunda Secundæ [the second part of the second part of his *Summa Theologiae*], the worthiness of a person can be considered in two ways. First, simply and in itself: and so he who is wiser and more virtuous is absolutely the better. Second, in comparison with the common good: and so it can happen that one who, speaking absolutely, is less good, that is, less virtuous and learned, is more useful to the common good by reason of his power or diligence or something of the kind. Since, then, the dispensing of spiritual things is ordered above all to the common benefit, for that reason the less good are sometimes preferred to the better in such matters without respect of persons. Further, according to the laws, for an election to be valid it is enough to choose one who is good and suitable. Nor need one choose the better according to the judicial forum [that is, as a court of law judges, as distinct from the forum of conscience]: otherwise an election could almost always be challenged. But as regards the conscience of the one who elects, he must choose the better, either simply or in comparison with the common good.

paras.t: Insuper dicit Albertus : Quod si quis honoret divitem magis quam pauperem propter lucra et commoda propria, quæ per hoc a divite consequi præstolatur, non potest esse sine peccato, si pauper propter suam paupertatem spernatur, et dives ei præhonoretur : quia ex hoc pauper scandalizatur, et datur ei occasio pusillanimitatis aut desperationis ex sua inopia.
paras.en: Albert says further that if someone honours the rich man more than the poor for the sake of his own gain and advantage, which he hopes to obtain from the rich man by doing so, it cannot be without sin, if the poor man is spurned for his poverty and the rich man honoured above him: for by this the poor man is scandalized, and is given occasion of faint-heartedness or of despair on account of his want.

paras.t: Dicendum ergo ad objectiones, quod si dives pauperi præponatur, et præhonoretur, non quia dives, sed ex aliqua rationabili causa, videlicet quia virtuosior, aut quia in potestate est constitutus, aut quia sapientior, aut senior, utilior, seu beneficentior, vel ut vitetur turbatio, non est personarum acceptio, nec peccatum, sed commendabile opus. Si autem ob solas divitias fiat hoc, et pauper (quia pauper est) postponatur, aut vilipendatur, vitiosum est, quamvis propter actus modicitatem possit interdum a mortali excusari. Interdum quoque videtur sufficere, ut pauper mentaliter honoretur.
paras.en: To the objections, then, it must be said that if a rich man is put before the poor and honoured above him, not because he is rich, but for some reasonable cause, namely because he is more virtuous, or because he is set in authority, or because he is wiser, or older, more useful, or more beneficent, or so that disturbance may be avoided, it is not respect of persons, nor a sin, but a commendable work. But if this is done for riches alone, and the poor man is put after him, or held cheap, because he is poor, it is wrong, although because the act is slight it can sometimes be excused from mortal sin. Sometimes too it seems enough that the poor man be honoured in the mind.

paras.t: Ad secundum dicendum, quod personarum acceptio tam in corporalibus quam in spiritualibus bonis committitur. Imo quum bona spiritualia sint corporalibus potiora, personarum acceptio in eis tanto vitiosior comprobatur, quanto hujusmodi bona sunt digniora. Amplius, personarum acceptio locum habet in exhibitione honoris. Quumque Deus altissimus sit primum et summum honorabile, cui debetur honor ratione suæ virtutis et sanctitatis, sapientiæ et causalitatis, beneficentiæ et dominationis, primævitatis ac dignitatis atque judiciariæ potestatis, constat quod rationalis creatura tanto est honorabilior, quanto in his magis Deo assimilatur, seu plus inde participat. Idcirco virtutibus præditi et sapientes sunt honorandi : similiter judices et prælati, quamvis iniqui ; senes quoque et parentes ; et homines universi, in quantum ad superdignissimæ Trinitatis imaginem similitudinemque creati, Christi sanguine liberati, ad supernaturalem beatitudinem ordinati, angelica custodia muniti, et maxime quia a Verbo æterno humana natura in unitate personæ est assumpta. Idcirco in homilia ait Gregorius, quod retunditur superbia nostra, quæ nescit in hominibus considerare dignitatem naturæ, qua ad Dei imaginem facti sunt.
paras.en: To the second it must be said that respect of persons is committed in bodily goods as well as in spiritual ones. Indeed, since spiritual goods are better than bodily ones, respect of persons in them is shown to be the more wicked, the more worthy such goods are. Moreover, respect of persons has a place in the showing of honour. And since God most high is the first and highest object of honour, to whom honour is owed by reason of his power and holiness, his wisdom and causality, his beneficence and dominion, his priority and dignity and his power of judgment, it is clear that a rational creature is the more worthy of honour, the more it is likened to God in these things, or the more it shares in them. Therefore those endowed with virtues, and the wise, are to be honoured; likewise judges and prelates, even if they are wicked; the old too, and parents; and all men, inasmuch as they are created to the image and likeness of the most high and worthy Trinity, set free by the blood of Christ, ordered to supernatural bliss, guarded by the angels, and above all because human nature was assumed by the eternal Word in the unity of a person. Therefore Gregory says in a homily that our pride is beaten down, which does not know how to consider in men the dignity of the nature by which they are made to the image of God.

paras.t: Sed quum Deus sit dives, sicut et potens, dicente Apostolo, Dives est in omnes et super omnes qui invocant eum : videtur quod divites sunt honorandi, secundum quod divites, et per suas divitias Deo assimilantur. Et respondendum, quia ut ait Augustinus primo de Civitate Dei, Deus dives est, non pecunia, sed omnipotentia. Denique dives est spirituali opulentia, videlicet perfectione, sanctitate, et beatitudine penitus infinita: ideo homo propter spirituales divitias, scilicet gratiam et virtutes, honorandus exsistit.
paras.en: But since God is rich as well as mighty, as the Apostle says: He is [[Rom 10:12|rich unto all|Dives est in omnes]] and over all [[Rom 10:12|that call upon him|qui invocant eum]], it seems that the rich are to be honoured insofar as they are rich, and are likened to God by their riches. And the answer is that, as Augustine says in the first book of the City of God, God is rich not in money but in omnipotence. Again, he is rich in spiritual wealth, namely in perfection, holiness and bliss wholly infinite: therefore a man is to be honoured for spiritual riches, that is, for grace and the virtues.

paras.t: Postremo videndum, an Deo conveniat personarum acceptio. Et videtur quod imo: quia quibusdam eodem modo dispositis, uni dat gratiam, et accipit eum, alium vero relinquit; imo frequenter graviores prævenit et convertit salvatque peccatores. Ad hoc Thomas respondet, quod duplex est datio. Una est actus justitiæ, qua aliquid alicui datur secundum dignitatem et meritum ejus: et circa illam attenditur acceptio personarum. Alia est actus liberalitatis, qua alicui aliquid gratis datur quod ei non debetur: et talis est collatio beneficiorum Dei, qui nulli est obligatus; et circa hanc non est personarum acceptio, quoniam unusquisque potest propria dare cui vult, et quantum vult, nisi in casu. Tamen Deus hoc maxime et irreprehensibiliter potest. Ideo apud eum locum non habet acceptio personarum, juxta illud Paralipomenon: Non est apud Dominum Deum nostrum iniquitas, nec personarum acceptio, nec acceptio munerum. Et in hoc, ipsum imitari debemus.
paras.en: Lastly, it must be seen whether respect of persons befits God. And it seems that it does: for of some who are disposed in the same way, he gives grace to one and accepts him, but leaves the other; indeed he often goes before the graver sinners and converts and saves them. To this Thomas replies that giving is twofold. One is an act of justice, by which something is given to someone according to his worthiness and merit: and respect of persons is found in regard to this. The other is an act of liberality, by which something is given to someone freely that is not owed to him: and such is the bestowing of God's benefits, who is bound to no one; and in regard to this there is no respect of persons, since anyone may give what is his own to whom he will and as much as he will, except in particular cases. And God can do this most of all, and beyond reproach. Therefore respect of persons has no place with him, according to that verse of Paralipomenon: [[2 Par 19:7|there is no iniquity with the Lord our God, nor respect of persons|Non est apud Dominum Deum nostrum iniquitas, nec personarum acceptio]], nor acceptance of gifts [Douay-Rheims: "nor desire of gifts"; Denis reads *acceptio munerum* for *cupido munerum*]. And in this we ought to imitate him.

paras.t: Nihilo minus adhuc propter duas causas dicitur apud Deum non esse acceptio personarum. Prima, quoniam nullum bonum relinquit irremuneratum, nec aliquem vere virtuosum refutat. Et hoc innuit princeps Apostolorum: In veritate, inquiens, comperi quoniam non est personarum acceptor Deus, sed in omni gente qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi. Secunda est, quoniam nulli quod in se est facienti Deus denegat gratiam. Idcirco apud Jeremiam ait: Quis est iste, qui applicet cor suum ut appropinquet mihi? Et in Job asseritur: Si direxerit homo ad Deum cor suum, spiritum illius et flatum ad se trahet. Et quia hæc duo ab hominibus communiter non servantur, merito ad discernendum inter perfectionem divinæ justitiæ, et imperfectionem fragilitatis humanæ, ait frequenter Scriptura quod apud Deum non est personarum acceptio.
paras.en: Nevertheless, it is said for two further reasons that there is no respect of persons with God. First, because he leaves no good unrewarded and rejects no one who is truly virtuous. And the prince of the Apostles indicates this: [[Acts 10:34|In very deed|In veritate]], he says, [[Acts 10:34|I perceive that God is not a respecter of persons|comperi quoniam non est personarum acceptor Deus]]: [[Acts 10:35|But in every nation, he that feareth him and worketh justice is acceptable to him|sed in omni gente qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi]]. The second is that God denies grace to no one who does what is in him. Therefore he says in Jeremias: [[Jer 30:21|who is this that setteth his heart to approach to me|Quis est iste, qui applicet cor suum ut appropinquet mihi?]]? And it is affirmed in Job: [[Job 34:14|If he turn his heart to him, he shall draw his spirit and breath unto himself|Si direxerit homo ad Deum cor suum, spiritum illius et flatum ad se trahet]] [Denis's text reads "If a man turn his heart to God"]. And because these two things are not commonly observed by men, Scripture rightly and often says, to distinguish between the perfection of divine justice and the imperfection of human frailty, that there is no respect of persons with God[[Deut 10:17||]][[2 Par 19:7||]][[Job 34:19||]].

paras.t: Insuper, quam periculosa sit personarum acceptio, imo quodcumque mortale peccatum, declarat apostolus Jacobus, subdens: Quicumque autem totam legem servaverit, id est, universa legis evangelicæ præcepta impleverit, offendat autem in uno, id est, post tantam justitiam transgrediatur unum præceptum Dei sive Ecclesiæ, seu unum incurrat peccatum mortale, per commissionem, quæ est contra præceptum negativum, vel omissionem, quæ est contra præceptum affirmativum, factus est omnium reus. Verbum hoc intricatum est valde. Ex eo siquidem sequi videtur, quod qui divitem pauperi præfert, aut furtum committit, reus sit hæreticæ pravitatis atque blasphemiæ, homicidii, adulterii, ceterorumque criminum; et quod tanta erit damnatio ejus qui unum solum commisit mortale, sicut ejus qui mille.
paras.en: Further, how dangerous respect of persons is, and indeed any mortal sin, the apostle James declares when he adds: [[2:10|And whosoever shall keep the whole law|Quicumque autem totam legem servaverit]], that is, shall fulfil all the commandments of the law of the Gospel, [[2:10|but offend in one point|offendat autem in uno]], that is, after so much justice shall transgress one commandment of God or of the Church, or fall into one mortal sin, by commission, which is against a negative commandment, or by omission, which is against an affirmative commandment, [[2:10|is become guilty of all|factus est omnium reus]]. This saying is very knotty. For it seems to follow from it that he who prefers a rich man to a poor one, or commits a theft, is guilty of heretical depravity and of blasphemy, of murder, of adultery and of all other crimes; and that the damnation of one who has committed only one mortal sin will be as great as that of one who has committed a thousand.

paras.t: Augustinus ergo et Beda exponunt, dicendo quod quia plenitudo legis est caritas, ideo omnis qui peccat, agit contra caritatem. Nec dicitur quis peccare, nisi contra caritatem Dei aut proximi operando, aut negligenter se habendo, præsertim quia in caritate præcepta omnia includuntur. Qui ergo offendit in uno, id est, contra caritatem agit, sive omittit id ad quod obligatur, factus est omnium reus, quoniam agit contra caritatem, in qua omnia pendent, tota videlicet lex et Prophetæ. Ista tamen solutio non est omnifarie plana. Quamvis enim qui unum committit mortale, violat caritatem, non tamen est reus omnium vitiorum, quæ sunt contra caritatem.
paras.en: Augustine and Bede, then, explain it by saying that because charity is [[Rom 13:10|the fulfilling of the law|plenitudo legis est]], everyone who sins acts against charity. Nor is anyone said to sin except by acting against the charity of God or of his neighbour, or by behaving negligently, especially since all the commandments are contained in charity. He, then, who offends in one, that is, acts against charity, or omits what he is bound to do, [[2:10|is become guilty of all|factus est omnium reus]], because he acts against charity, on which all things depend, namely [[Matt 22:40|the whole law and the prophets|tota videlicet lex et Prophetæ]]. This solution, however, is not in every way plain. For although he who commits one mortal sin violates charity, he is not for all that guilty of all the vices that are against charity.

paras.t: Porro Albertus exponit, dicendo quod in peccato duo considerantur: unum formale, quod est a summo bono aversio; aliud materiale, quod est conversio inordinata ad bonum commutabile et caducum. Quum ergo omnia peccata sint ab uno summo aversiva, ex parte hujus aversionis, et ex parte boni summi a quo avertunt, habent quamdam connexionem et unitatem. Itaque qui offendit in uno, dicitur omnium reus fieri, quia fit reus in tali aversione a Deo, per cujus aversionem omnia peccata habent formaliter ut sint peccata, et quodammodo unum peccatum sunt, quemadmodum, juxta Gregorium, omnia præcepta unum dicuntur in radice caritatis. Sed his obstat, quia secundum doctores concorditer, quamvis virtutes connexæ sint, non tamen peccata.
paras.en: Albert, again, explains it by saying that two things are considered in sin: one formal, which is the turning away from the highest good; the other material, which is the disordered turning towards a changeable and perishable good [the classic *aversio a Deo* and *conversio ad creaturam*]. Since, then, all sins turn away from the one highest good, on the side of this turning away, and on the side of the highest good from which they turn away, they have a certain connection and unity. And so he who offends in one is said to become guilty of all, because he becomes guilty in such a turning away from God, by which turning away all sins have formally that they are sins, and in a manner are one sin; just as, according to Gregory, all the commandments are said to be one in the root of charity. But against this stands the fact that, according to the doctors with one accord, though the virtues are connected, the sins are not.

paras.t: Alii ergo exponunt, dicentes (sicut magister Nicolaus de Lyra specialiter) quod offendens in uno, fit omnium reus quantum ad pœnam damni, quæ est divinæ carentia visionis: quam homo meretur atque incurrit per unam transgressionem divinæ legis; sed pœnam incurrit majorem, qui plures transgressiones divinæ legis commisit. Huic expositioni objici potest, quod etiam per unamquamque divinæ legis transgressionem, homo incurrit pœnam sensus, quemadmodum pœnam damni.
paras.en: Others, then, explain it (as Master Nicholas of Lyra in particular) by saying that he who offends in one becomes guilty of all as to the pain of loss [*pœna damni*, the loss of God, as distinct from the *pœna sensus*, the pain of sense], which is the lack of the vision of God: which a man merits and incurs by one transgression of the divine law; but he who has committed several transgressions of the divine law incurs a greater punishment. Against this explanation it can be objected that by each transgression of the divine law a man incurs the pain of sense, just as he does the pain of loss.

paras.t: Aliter dici potest, quod in uno offendens, fit omnium reus, non formaliter, sed quodammodo æquivalenter in genere, in quantum per unum mortale perduntur charismata gratiæ in præsenti et dona gloriæ in futuro, pœna quoque damni et pœna sensus in inferno infliguntur, sicut per multa seu omnia. Potest quoque clarius sic exponi: Qui offendit in uno, fit omnium reus, id est, omnium præteritorum operum suorum virtuosorum merito mox privatur, quemadmodum per Ezechielem Dominus protestatur: Si averterit se justus, et fecerit iniquitatem, omnes justitiæ quas fecerit, non recordabuntur; in prævaricatione sua morietur.
paras.en: It can be said otherwise, that he who offends in one becomes guilty of all, not formally, but in a manner equivalently in kind, inasmuch as by one mortal sin the gifts of grace in the present and the gifts of glory in the future are lost, and the pain of loss and the pain of sense are inflicted in hell, just as by many sins or by all. It can also be explained more clearly thus: He who offends in one becomes guilty of all; that is, he is at once deprived of the merit of all his past virtuous works, as the Lord declares through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:24|if the just man turn himself away|Si averterit se justus]], [[Ezech 18:24|and do iniquity|et fecerit iniquitatem]], [[Ezech 18:24|all his justices which he hath done, shall not be remembered|omnes justitiæ quas fecerit, non recordabuntur]]: [[Ezech 18:24|in the prevarication|in prævaricatione sua]] [[Ezech 18:24|he shall die|morietur]].

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Qui enim dixit, Non mœchaberis; dixit et, Non occides, id est, qui fornicationem prohibuit, prohibuit et homicidium. Quod si non mœchaberis, occides autem, id est, contra præceptum de mœchatione vitanda non feceris, sed præceptum de homicidio fugiendo infregeris, factus es transgressor legis divinæ, ejus violando præceptum. Idcirco spiritualiter mortuus es, et opera tua præterita meritoria, sunt mortificata, esque privatus omni charismate gratiæ ac virtutum, ac si omnia violasses præcepta: quamvis non sis tam enormis transgressor, nec ita induratus, neque tam difficulter curabilis, sed nec tantæ damnationi obnoxius, ut ille qui plura aut omnia violavit præcepta.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[2:11|For he that said: Thou shalt not commit adultery, said also: Thou shalt not kill|Qui enim dixit, Non mœchaberis; dixit et, Non occides]]; that is, he who forbade fornication forbade murder also. [[2:11|Now if thou do not commit adultery, but shalt kill|Quod si non mœchaberis, occides autem]], that is, if thou hast not acted against the commandment to avoid adultery, but hast broken the commandment to shun murder, [[2:11|thou art become a transgressor of the law|factus es transgressor legis]] of God, by violating his commandment. Therefore thou art spiritually dead, and thy past meritorious works are deadened, and thou art deprived of every gift of grace and of the virtues, as if thou hadst violated all the commandments: although thou art not so enormous a transgressor, nor so hardened, nor so hard to cure, nor yet liable to so great a damnation, as he who has violated several or all of the commandments.

paras.t: Quum ergo tam ardua sit via salutis, rite subjungitur: Sic loquimini, et sic facite, id est, tam discreti, tam virtuosi ac fervidi sitis, in verbis et factis, sicut per legem libertatis, id est per legem evangelicam (quæ cur lex libertatis dicatur, expositum est), incipientes judicari, id est, ac si statim essetis judicandi a Deo per evangelicam legem, hoc est juxta tenorem et obligationem evangelicæ legis: quæ quanto ceteris legibus est perfectior, tanto ad virtuosiorem vitam suos obligat professores, quum juxta doctrinam Apostoli, debeat unusquisque digne conversari vocatione qua vocatus est. Quemadmodum ergo professores legis Moysis tenebantur perfectius vivere, quam solam naturalem legem habentes; sic Christiani ad perfectiorem adstricti sunt vitam, quam in veteri lege tenebantur Judæi: præsertim quia et ampliora ac eminentiora beneficia desuper exhibita sunt populo christiano, quam Judæis in veteri Testamento, aut gentilibus in lege naturæ. Ideo Christiani Deo subjectiores, devotiores, et gratiores esse tenentur, dicente Gregorio: Quum augentur dona, rationes etiam crescunt donorum. Alioqui Christiani gravius judicabuntur per legem libertatis, quam Judæi per legem scriptam, aut gentes per legem naturalem. Nam teste Apostolo, Quicumque in lege peccaverint, per legem judicabuntur. Hinc ad Hebræos inducitur: Abundantius oportet nos observare ea quæ audivimus, ne forte perfluamus. Si enim qui per angelos dictus est sermo, factus est firmus, et omnis prævaricatio et inobedientia accepit justam mercedis retributionem: quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem? Hinc ait et Christus: Cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo.
paras.en: Since, then, the way of salvation is so arduous, it is fittingly added: [[2:12|So speak ye and so do|Sic loquimini, et sic facite]], that is, be so discreet, so virtuous and fervent in words and deeds, even as [[2:12|by the law of liberty|per legem libertatis]], that is, by the law of the Gospel (why it is called the law of liberty has been explained), [[2:12|being to be judged|incipientes judicari]], that is, as if you were straightway to be judged by God through the law of the Gospel, that is, according to the tenor and obligation of the law of the Gospel: which, the more perfect it is than the other laws, the more it binds those who profess it to a more virtuous life, since according to the Apostle's teaching each one ought to live worthily of the vocation to which he has been called[[Eph 4:1||]]. As, then, those who professed the law of Moses were bound to live more perfectly than those who had the natural law alone, so Christians are bound to a more perfect life than the Jews were bound to in the old law: above all because both ampler and more eminent benefits have been shown from on high to the Christian people than to the Jews in the Old Testament, or to the gentiles in the law of nature. Therefore Christians are bound to be more subject, more devout and more grateful to God, as Gregory says: When gifts are increased, the reckoning for the gifts grows too. Otherwise Christians will be judged more heavily by the law of liberty than the Jews by the written law, or the gentiles by the natural law. For, as the Apostle witnesses, [[Rom 2:12|whosoever have sinned in the law shall be judged by the law|Quicumque in lege peccaverint, per legem judicabuntur]]. Hence it is put to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:1|ought we more diligently to observe the things which we have heard lest perhaps we should let them slip|Abundantius oportet nos observare ea quæ audivimus, ne forte perfluamus]]. [[Heb 2:2|For if the word spoken by angels became steadfast and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward:|Si enim qui per angelos dictus est sermo, factus est firmus, et omnis prævaricatio et inobedientia accepit justam mercedis retributionem]] [[Heb 2:3|How shall we escape if we neglect so great salvation?|quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem?]] Hence Christ too says: [[Luke 12:48|unto whomsoever much is given, of him much shall be required|Cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo]] [Denis has *plus … plus*, "more … more"].

paras.t: Præterea quod Jacobus ait apostolus, Sicut per legem libertatis incipientes judicari, potest et exponi de judicio approbationis seu reprobationis ac discretionis, quo Deus indesinenter in se ipso approbat eos qui bene vivunt, et detestatur inique agentes, atque inter justos et injustos discernit. Futuræ etiam retributionis quemdam prægustum jam quoque interdum suis præstat electis. Hinc apud Jeremiam habetur: Domine Deus fortissime, magnus consilio et incomprehensibilis cogitatu, cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam, ut reddas unicuique secundum vias suas. Et Psalmista: Oculi, inquit, Domini super justos, et aures ejus in preces eorum; vultus autem Domini super facientes mala. In Ecclesiastico quoque legitur: Oculi Domini multo plus lucidiores sunt super solem, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum. Ideo sanctus Job dixit: Nonne Deus considerat viam meam, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat?
paras.en: Moreover, what the apostle James says, [[2:12|as being to be judged by the law of liberty|Sicut per legem libertatis incipientes judicari]], can also be explained of the judgment of approval or reproval and of discernment, by which God unceasingly in himself approves those who live well, and detests those who act wickedly, and discerns between the just and the unjust. Sometimes, too, he already gives his elect a certain foretaste of the retribution to come. Hence we have in Jeremias: [[Jer 32:17|O Lord God|Domine Deus]], [[Jer 32:18|most mighty|fortissime]], [[Jer 32:19|Great in counsel, and incomprehensible in thought: whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the children of Adam, to render unto every one according to his ways|magnus consilio et incomprehensibilis cogitatu, cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam, ut reddas unicuique secundum vias suas]] [Denis has "upon all the children of Adam"]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:16|The eyes|Oculi]], says he, [[Ps 33:16|of the Lord are upon the just: and his ears unto their prayers|Domini super justos, et aures ejus in preces eorum]]; [[Ps 33:17|But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things|vultus autem Domini super facientes mala]]. In Ecclesiasticus too we read: [[Ecclus 23:28|the eyes of the Lord are far brighter than the sun, beholding round about all the ways of men|Oculi Domini multo plus lucidiores sunt super solem, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum]]. Therefore holy Job said: [[Job 31:4|Doth not he consider my ways, and number all my steps?|Nonne Deus considerat viam meam, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat?]]

paras.t: Postremo, fideles incipiunt in hac vita per legem evangelicam judicari a suis superioribus ac prælatis; et qui eorum correptionem ac correctionem patienter ac obedienter suscipiunt, divini judicii evadent rigorem, quum et Apostolus fateatur: Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur.
paras.en: Lastly, the faithful begin in this life to be judged by the law of the Gospel by their superiors and prelates; and those who receive their rebuke and correction patiently and obediently will escape the rigour of the divine judgment, since the Apostle too declares: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]].

paras.t: Et quia lex evangelica opera misericordiæ præsertim commendat ac præcipit, Christiani in verbis et factis debent esse misericordes. Propter quod subditur: Judicium enim sine misericordia fiet a Deo illi homini, qui non fecerit misericordiam proximis suis in vita præsenti, antequam tribunali præsentetur divino. Quemadmodum enim beati misericordes, quoniam misericordiam consequentur; sic infelices sunt immisericordes, quoniam misericordiam non obtinebunt, sed juste ac terribiliter damnabuntur, quemadmodum dives epulo, qui misereri noluit Lazaro. Hinc loquitur Judex summus: Nolite judicare, et non judicabimini; nolite condemnare, et non condemnabimini; dimittite, et dimittemini: qua mensura mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis. Et iterum: Si non dimiseritis, nec Pater meus cœlestis dimittet vobis peccata vestra. Unde et servo qui suo conservo non fuit misericors, dominus ait: Serve nequam, omne debitum dimisi tibi, quoniam rogasti me. Nonne ergo oportuit et te misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego tui misertus sum? Iratusque dominus, tradidit servum illum tortoribus, quoadusque redderet debitum universum. Unde quanto unicuique major misericordia a Deo impensa est, tanto proximis suis misericordior esse debet. — Sed his objici potest, quia ut ait Propheta, Universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas. Quocirca dicunt doctores, et super quartum Sententiarum declarant, quod in omni opere Dei misericordia et justitia commiscentur, ita quod etiam reprobi citra condignum in infernis puniuntur. Et respondendum, quod immisericordibus dicitur fieri judicium sine misericordia, non quod nulla eis miseratio fiat, sed quia singularis rigor judicialis fit eis, et ipsa justitia in eorum dijudicatione ac punitione æternaliter cum speciali evidentia prædominans erit, secundum quod homo sua crudelitate specialiter meruerit.
paras.en: And because the law of the Gospel above all commends and commands the works of mercy, Christians ought to be merciful in words and deeds. Wherefore it is added: [[2:13|For judgment without mercy|Judicium enim sine misericordia]] shall be done by God [[2:13|to him that hath not done mercy|illi homini, qui non fecerit misericordiam]] to his neighbours in the present life, before he is presented at the divine tribunal. For as [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful|beati misericordes]], for they [[Matt 5:7|shall obtain mercy|misericordiam consequentur]], so the unmerciful are unhappy, for they will not obtain mercy, but will be justly and terribly damned, like the rich feaster who would not have mercy on Lazarus[[Luke 16:19||]]. Hence the supreme Judge says: [[Luke 6:37|Judge not: and you shall not be judged. Condemn not: and you shall not be condemned. Forgive: and you shall be forgiven.|Nolite judicare, et non judicabimini; nolite condemnare, et non condemnabimini; dimittite, et dimittemini]] [[Luke 6:38|with the same measure that you shall mete withal, it shall be measured to you again|qua mensura mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis]]. And again: [[Matt 6:15|if you will not forgive men, neither will your Father forgive you your offences|Si non dimiseritis, nec Pater meus cœlestis dimittet vobis peccata vestra]] [Denis has "neither will my heavenly Father forgive you"]. Hence also to the servant who was not merciful to his fellow servant the lord says: [[Matt 18:32|Thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all the debt, because thou besoughtest me|Serve nequam, omne debitum dimisi tibi, quoniam rogasti me]]. [[Matt 18:33|Shouldst not thou then have had compassion also on thy fellow servant, even as I had compassion on thee?|Nonne ergo oportuit et te misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego tui misertus sum?]] [[Matt 18:34|And his lord being angry, delivered him to the torturers until he paid all the debt.|Iratusque dominus, tradidit servum illum tortoribus, quoadusque redderet debitum universum]] Hence the greater the mercy God has shown to each one, the more merciful he ought to be to his neighbours. — But against this it can be objected that, as the Prophet says, [[Ps 24:10|All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth|Universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas]]. For this reason the doctors say, and declare on the fourth book of the Sentences, that in every work of God mercy and justice are mingled, so that even the reprobate are punished in hell less than they deserve. And the answer is that judgment without mercy is said to be done to the unmerciful not because no compassion at all is shown them, but because a singular judicial rigour is applied to them, and justice itself will prevail eternally in their judgment and punishment with a special evidence, according as a man has specially deserved it by his cruelty.

paras.t: Ex his innotescit, quam pronus ac fervidus esse debeat unusquisque pro viribus suis ad corporalia ac spiritualia misericordiæ opera: quia ut ait Scriptura, Qui pronus est ad misericordiam, benedicetur. Et Christus in Evangelio loquitur: Estote misericordes, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis misericors est. Et denuo protestatur, reprobos in die judicii ideo condemnandos, quia misericordiæ opera non fecerint.
paras.en: From this it is made known how inclined and fervent each one ought to be, according to his strength, to the corporal and spiritual works of mercy: for, as Scripture says, [[Prov 22:9|He that is inclined to mercy, shall be blessed|Qui pronus est ad misericordiam, benedicetur]]. And Christ says in the Gospel: [[Luke 6:36|Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.|Estote misericordes, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis misericors est]] [Denis adds *cœlestis*, "heavenly"]. And again he declares that the reprobate are to be condemned on the day of judgment for this, that they have not done the works of mercy[[Matt 25:41||]].

paras.t: Superexaltat autem misericordia judicium (vel, ut alii legunt, judicio), id est, plus placet Deo caritativa miseratio, quam judicialis districtio; nisi forte in certo casu, propter bonum commune et conservationem justitiæ, oporteat districtionem judicii exercere: quod tamen cum interna pietate atque ex caritate agendum est. Hinc et jura sunt pia et ad misericordiam magis prona, magisque stant juramento accusati, quam accusantis; atque in dubiis casibus ad misericordiæ partem est declinandum. Potest et ita exponi: Superexaltat misericordia judicium, id est, transcendit, et magis apparet in operibus Dei misericordia ejus quam rigor judicii, præsertim in vita hac, juxta id Psalmistæ: Suavis Dominus universis, et miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Unde per Ezechielem ait: Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii, et non magis ut convertatur et vivat? Imo, ut loquitur Isaias, ulcisci et punire est peregrinum et alienum ab eo, cujus natura est bonitas, cujus proprietas pietas. Superexaltat demum misericordia judicium, quia misericordia Dei relucet in electis et salvatis in cœlo, judicium vero in reprobis ac damnatis in tartaro.
paras.en: [[2:13|And mercy exalteth itself above judgment|Superexaltat autem misericordia judicium]] (or, as others read, *judicio* [that is, the dative, "exalts itself over judgment"]), that is, charitable compassion pleases God more than judicial severity; unless perhaps in a certain case, for the common good and the preservation of justice, the severity of judgment must be exercised: which nevertheless must be done with inward tenderness and out of charity. Hence the laws too are tender and more inclined to mercy, and they stand more by the oath of the accused than of the accuser; and in doubtful cases one must lean to the side of mercy. It can also be explained thus: [[2:13|mercy exalteth itself above judgment|Superexaltat misericordia judicium]], that is, surpasses it; and in the works of God his mercy appears more than the rigour of judgment, especially in this life, according to that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 144:9|The Lord is sweet to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.|Suavis Dominus universis, et miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus]] [the margin gives only Ps. cxliv]. Hence he says through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:23|Is it my will that a sinner should die|Numquid voluntatis meæ est mors impii]], [[Ezech 18:23|and not that he should be converted|et non magis ut convertatur]] [[Ezech 18:23|and live|et vivat]]? Nay, as Isaias says, to take vengeance and to punish is strange and foreign to him whose nature is goodness, whose property is tenderness[[Is 28:21||]]. Finally, [[2:13|mercy exalteth itself above judgment|Superexaltat demum misericordia judicium]], because the mercy of God shines forth in the elect and the saved in heaven, but his judgment in the reprobate and the damned in hell.

paras.t: Consequenter docet Apostolus fidem informem non sufficere ad salutem. Et dicitur fides informis, quæ non est caritate formata, ac bonis operibus decorata in adultis et tempore opportuno. Quid proderit, fratres mei, si fidem quis dicat se habere, opera autem non habeat, id est, per fidem non bene vivat, implendo præcepta, et fidem decorando per meritoria gesta? Numquid poterit fides salvare eum, id est instrumentaliter ad salutem perducere? quasi dicat, Nequaquam. Imo reddit eum magis damnabilem, quoniam servus sciens voluntatem domini sui, et non faciens, plagis vapulabit multis. Ideo malus Christianus gravius condemnatur quam infidelis, ceteris paribus.
paras.en: Next the Apostle teaches that unformed faith does not suffice for salvation. And that faith is called unformed [that is, faith without charity, which gives faith its "form" or life] which is not formed by charity and adorned with good works, in adults and at the fitting time. [[2:14|What shall it profit, my brethren, if a man say he hath faith, but hath not works?|Quid proderit, fratres mei, si fidem quis dicat se habere, opera autem non habeat]] That is: if he does not live well through faith, fulfilling the commandments and adorning faith with meritorious deeds. [[2:14|Shall faith be able to save him|Numquid poterit fides salvare eum]], that is, lead him instrumentally to salvation? As if to say: By no means. Nay, it makes him more damnable, since [[Luke 12:47|that servant, who knew the will of his lord|servus sciens voluntatem domini sui]], and did not do it, [[Luke 12:47|shall be beaten with many stripes|plagis vapulabit multis]]. Therefore a bad Christian is condemned more heavily than an unbeliever, other things being equal.

paras.t: Deinde ostendit per simile, fidem talem neminem posse perducere ad salutem. Si autem frater aut soror, id est proximus, cujuscumque sint sexus, nudi sint, et in[…] dicat autem aliquis de vobis illis: Ite in pace, calefiamini et saturamini, id est, bene tractemini; non dederitis autem eis quæ necessaria sunt corpori: quid proderit? Utique nihil, quia pulchra verba absque reali subventione non sufficiunt indigenti. Tamen, si aliquis habeat desiderium succurrendi egeno, sed non habeat facultatem, et tunc det consolatorium ac informatorium verbum, laudabile est atque proficuum, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Nonne ardorem refrigerabit ros? Sic et verbum melius quam datum. Nonne ecce verbum super datum bonum? Et iterum scriptum est: Congregationi pauperum te affabilem facito.
paras.en: Then he shows by a comparison that such faith can lead no one to salvation. [[2:15|And if a brother or sister|Si autem frater aut soror]], that is, a neighbour, of whichever sex, [[2:15|be naked|nudi sint]], and […] [the transcription breaks off after "et in-"; the rest of v. 15, "and want daily food", is not in the text], [[2:16|And one of you say to them: Go in peace, be ye warmed and filled|dicat autem aliquis de vobis illis: Ite in pace, calefiamini et saturamini]], that is, may you be well treated; [[2:16|yet give them not those things that are necessary for the body, what shall it profit?|non dederitis autem eis quæ necessaria sunt corpori: quid proderit?]] Nothing at all, since fine words without real help do not suffice for one in need. Yet if someone has the desire to help the needy but has not the means, and then gives a word of comfort and instruction, it is praiseworthy and profitable, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:16|Shall not the dew assuage the heat? so also the good word is better than the gift.|Nonne ardorem refrigerabit ros? Sic et verbum melius quam datum]] [[Ecclus 18:17|Lo, is not a word better than a gift|Nonne ecce verbum super datum bonum]]? [the margin reads Eccli. xxviii, 16, 17; the words are Ecclus 18:16–17] And again it is written: [[Ecclus 4:7|Make thyself affable to the congregation of the poor|Congregationi pauperum te affabilem facito]] [the margin reference here could not be read].

paras.t: Sic et fides si non habeat opera, id est exsecutionem præceptorum, loco et tempore opportuno, mortua est in semetipsa. Porro, per opera in hoc loco, non solum intelligenda sunt opera exteriora, sed indifferenter quicumque actus virtuosi ex virtute eliciti aut imperati, sive sint interiores, sive exteriores. Nam et in Evangelio sumitur opus pro opere interiori, quum dicitur: Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum quem misit ille. In Job autem pro interiori exteriorique opere sumitur, quum dicitur: Opus hominis reddet ei Deus. Staret enim in casu, quod alicui sufficerent ad salutem interiores fidei actus, ut credere in Deum. Itaque, sicut in exterioribus dicitur aliquid mortuum, quod caret sensu et motu; sic fides sensu carens interno, seu caritatis sensificatione (qua homini sapit Deus, et veritas prima cui innititur fides, dulcescit), et quæ bonæ ac meritoriæ actionis motum non habet, recte mortua perhibetur, non vivificans spiritualiter suum subjectum, nec excitans illud ad actum. Et hæc vocatur fides informis, utpote caritate non decorata. Fides autem per dilectionem operans, viva vocatur. Tamen quantum ad substantiam, utraque fides eadem perhibetur. Nam per mortale peccatum, suam, quam habuit a caritate, amittit formationem, decorationem et vivificationem; sed caritate per pœnitentiam redeunte, rursus formatur et vivificatur. Unde quod in Marco legitur, Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit, de fide formata accipitur.
paras.en: [[2:17|So faith also, if it have not works|Sic et fides si non habeat opera]], that is, the carrying out of the commandments in the fitting place and time, [[2:17|is dead in itself|mortua est in semetipsa]]. Further, by *works* in this place are to be understood not only outward works, but without distinction any virtuous acts elicited or commanded by a virtue [that is, acts produced by the virtue itself, or done at its bidding by another power], whether they be inward or outward. For in the Gospel too *work* is taken for an inward work, when it is said: [[John 6:29|This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he hath sent|Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum quem misit ille]]. But in Job it is taken for inward and outward work, when it is said: [[Job 34:11|he will render to a man his work|Opus hominis reddet ei Deus]]. For it could be the case that the inward acts of faith, such as believing in God, would suffice someone for salvation. And so, as among outward things that is called dead which lacks sense and motion, so faith that lacks inward sense, or the quickening sense of charity (by which God has savour for a man, and the first truth, on which faith rests, grows sweet), and has not the motion of good and meritorious action, is rightly said to be dead, not quickening its subject spiritually nor rousing it to act. And this is called unformed faith, as not adorned with charity. But [[Gal 5:6|faith that worketh by Charity|Fides autem per dilectionem operans]] is called living [Denis has *dilectionem* for the Vulgate's *caritatem*]. Yet as to its substance both faiths are said to be the same. For through mortal sin faith loses the formation, adornment and quickening it had from charity; but when charity returns through penance, it is formed and quickened again. Hence what we read in Mark, [[Mark 16:16|He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved|Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit]], is taken of formed faith.

paras.t: Sed dicet quis, id est, aliquis fidem et opera fidei habens, dicere potest ad proximum: Tu fidem habes sine operibus, et ego opera habeo simul cum fide; ostende mihi fidem tuam sine operibus: quasi improperatorie dicat, Hoc facere nequis, ideo fides tua hujusmodi non sufficit tibi; et ego ostendam tibi fidem meam ex operibus, id est, per opera fidei quæ exerceo, probabiliter tibi ostendam me fidem habere. Verumtamen non sine revelatione certitudinaliter scire quis potest se fidem formatam habere ex suis operibus, quamvis scire possit se esse in fide, eo quod fidei formatæ caritas sit annexa.
paras.en: [[2:18|But some man will say|Sed dicet quis]], that is, someone who has faith and the works of faith can say to his neighbour: [[2:18|Thou hast faith|Tu fidem habes]] without works, [[2:18|and I have works|et ego opera habeo]] together with faith; [[2:18|Shew me thy faith without works|ostende mihi fidem tuam sine operibus]]: as if he said reproachfully, This you cannot do, therefore such faith of yours does not suffice you; [[2:18|and I will shew thee, by works, my faith|et ego ostendam tibi fidem meam ex operibus]], that is, by the works of faith that I practise I will show you, as a probable sign, that I have faith. Yet without a revelation no one can know with certainty from his works that he has formed faith, although he can know that he is in the faith, since charity is joined to formed faith.

paras.t: Tu credis quoniam unus est Deus, id est, unum esse Deum tu credis. Quod tamen per naturalem rationem sciri potest ac demonstrari, quamvis eo modo quo unum esse Deum fides tenet catholica, non sit naturali ratione tam certum atque probabile, utpote, unum verum Deum esse, omnium provisorem, gubernatorem, universa et singula distinctissime cognoscentem ac judicantem. Bene facis, ita credendo. Quamvis illud credere non sit meritorium, quia ex caritate non oritur, sed ex fide informi, est tamen quoddam bonum ex genere, sicut eleemosynam dare. Sumitur autem Facere, hoc loco, pro actu interiori, quia credere unum esse Deum, est actus interior. Communiter vero accipitur Facere, pro actione extra manante seu in exteriorem tendente materiam, Agere autem, pro actione immanente. Et dæmones credunt, et contremiscunt. Idcirco non sufficit nuda fides, nec quæcumque fidei opera, quum dæmones non solum credant, sed etiam timeant servili timore. Nec solum credunt unum esse Deum, sed eumdem etiam credunt trinum consistere in personis, et quidquid ad catholicam pertinet fidem. Legitur enim in Luca dæmon dixisse: Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu Nazarene? Scio te quod sis Sanctus Dei. Et ibidem legitur: Exibant dæmonia multa, clamantia et dicentia: Quia tu es Filius Dei. Ait hoc loco venerabilis Beda: Qui Deum non credunt, aut creditum non verentur, profecto dæmonibus tardiores ac proterviores sunt æstimandi. Sed nec, Deum credere et contremiscere, magnum est, si non et in eum credatur, hoc est, per fidem caritate formatam in eum tendatur, et ejus in corde amor servetur. — Quæritur, an dæmones habeant fidem. Respondet Albertus: Fides proprie est de non visis, et de his ad quorum investigationem humana ratio non pertingit. Ad quæ credenda potest aliquis moveri dupliciter: Primo, ex habitu fidei divinitus sibi infuso: et ita non est in dæmonibus fides. Secundo, ex aliquibus evidentibus signis atque miraculis, quæ quum soli Deo sint possibilia, et ad fidei confirmationem copiose sint facta, dæmones naturali acumine intellectuali vigentes, inde cognoscunt fidei veritatem. Imo credere compelluntur ex evidentia talium argumentorum, secundum quod intellectus dicitur cogi. Sicque dæmonum fides non est virtus infusa, nec ex voluntatis libertate ac caritate, sed potius ex violentia rationis. Hanc autem quæstionem Thomas in secunda secundæ, quæstione 5, plenius tractat: et consonat ejus responsio responsioni inductæ.
paras.en: [[2:19|Thou believest that there is one God|Tu credis quoniam unus est Deus]], that is, thou believest that God is one. This, however, can be known and demonstrated by natural reason, although in the way in which the Catholic faith holds that God is one it is not so certain and provable by natural reason: namely, that there is one true God, the provider and governor of all things, knowing and judging all things together and each one most distinctly. [[2:19|Thou dost well|Bene facis]] in so believing. Although that believing is not meritorious, since it does not spring from charity but from unformed faith, it is nevertheless a certain good in its kind [that is, an act good by its object, though not meritorious], like giving alms. Now *to do* [*facere*] is taken in this place for an inward act, since to believe that God is one is an inward act. But commonly *to do* is taken for an action that passes outward or tends to outward matter, and *to act* [*agere*] for an immanent action. [[2:19|the devils also believe and tremble|Et dæmones credunt, et contremiscunt]]. Therefore bare faith does not suffice, nor any works of faith whatever, since the devils not only believe but also fear with servile fear. Nor do they believe only that God is one, but also that the same God subsists as three in persons, and whatever belongs to the Catholic faith. For we read in Luke that a devil said: [[Luke 4:34|What have we to do with thee, Jesus of Nazareth?|Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu Nazarene?]] [[Luke 4:34|I know thee who thou art, the holy one of God|Scio te quod sis Sanctus Dei]]. And in the same place we read: [[Luke 4:41|And devils went out from many, crying out and saying: Thou art the son of God|Exibant dæmonia multa, clamantia et dicentia: Quia tu es Filius Dei]]. The Venerable Bede says on this place: Those who do not believe in God, or, believing, do not revere him, must surely be reckoned slower and more insolent than the devils. But neither is it a great thing to believe God and to tremble, unless one also believes *in* him, that is, tends to him by faith formed by charity, and keeps his love in the heart. — It is asked whether the devils have faith. Albert answers: Faith is properly of things not seen, and of those to whose investigation human reason does not reach. To believe these, someone can be moved in two ways. First, by the habit of faith infused into him by God: and in this way there is no faith in the devils. Secondly, by certain evident signs and miracles, which, since they are possible to God alone and have been done in abundance to confirm the faith, the devils, strong in natural sharpness of intellect, thereby know the truth of the faith. Nay, they are compelled to believe by the evidence of such proofs, in the sense in which the intellect is said to be forced. And so the faith of the devils is not an infused virtue, nor does it come from freedom of will and from charity, but rather from the compulsion of reason. Thomas treats this question more fully in the *Secunda Secundæ*, question 5; and his answer agrees with the one given.

paras.t: Vis autem scire, o homo inanis, id est vanus et spiritualiter vacuus, utpote fidei opera et caritatem non habens, et per consequens ad ultimi finis adeptionem indispositus et ineptus (dicitur enim inane, quod non consequitur debitum finem), quoniam fides sine operibus mortua est?
paras.en: [[2:20|But wilt thou know, O vain man|Vis autem scire, o homo inanis]], that is, empty and spiritually void, as having neither the works of faith nor charity, and in consequence undisposed and unfit for attaining the last end (for that is called *inane*, empty, which does not attain its due end), [[2:20|that faith without works is dead?|quoniam fides sine operibus mortua est?]]

paras.t: Abraham pater noster: qui omnium fidelium pater spiritualiter vocatur per fidei et virtutum imitationem. Et fidelium Judæorum spiritualis atque carnalis exstitit pater, infidelium autem Judæorum solum carnalis pater fuit. Unde dicitur ad Galatas: Qui ex fide sunt, hi sunt filii Abrahæ. Et in Joanne ait Salvator: Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite. Nonne ex operibus justificatus est, id est justior factus, atque a Deo sublimiter commendatus ac approbatus, offerens, id est, ad offerendum paratum se exhibens ac disponens, Isaac filium suum super altare? Colligavit enim eum, et posuit super struem lignorum.
paras.en: [[2:21|Abraham our father|Abraham pater noster]]: who is called spiritually the father of all the faithful, through the imitation of his faith and virtues. And he was the spiritual and the carnal father of the faithful Jews, but of the unbelieving Jews only the carnal father. Hence it is said to the Galatians: [[Gal 3:7|they who are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham|Qui ex fide sunt, hi sunt filii Abrahæ]]. And in John the Saviour says: [[John 8:39|If you be the children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham|Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite]]. Was he not [[2:21|justified by works|Nonne ex operibus justificatus est]], that is, made more just, and highly commended and approved by God, [[2:21|offering up|offerens]], that is, showing and disposing himself ready to offer, [[2:21|Isaac his son upon the altar|Isaac filium suum super altare]]? For he bound him and laid him upon the pile of wood[[Gen 22:9||]].

paras.t: Vides, id est, ex his intelligere debes, quoniam fides cooperabatur operibus illius. Fides enim est oculus rationis, dirigens in agendis, et opera ad ultimum referens finem, qui sola fide, non clare per speciem in hac vita conspicitur. Et ex operibus fides consummata est, id est, fides Abrahæ per obedientiam ejus et ea quæ circa Isaac Deo jubente exercuit, actuationem et complementum accepit. Habitus namque et actus ipsius se mutuo ornant ac roborant: quia ex habitu actus procedit, et habitum actus ejus stabilit et conservat ac perficit.
paras.en: [[2:22|Seest thou|Vides]], that is, from this thou oughtest to understand, [[2:22|that faith did cooperate with his works|quoniam fides cooperabatur operibus illius]]. For faith is the eye of reason, directing it in what is to be done, and referring works to the last end, which in this life is seen by faith alone, not clearly by sight. [[2:22|and by works faith was made perfect|Et ex operibus fides consummata est]], that is, the faith of Abraham received its actuation and completion through his obedience and what he did concerning Isaac at God's command. For a habit and its act adorn and strengthen each other: since the act proceeds from the habit, and its act establishes, preserves and perfects the habit.

paras.t: Et suppleta, id est verificata ac aliis manifeste probata, est Scriptura Geneseos dicens: Credidit Abraham Deo dicenti ad eum: Suspice cælum, et numera stellas ejus, si potes: sic erit semen tuum; et reputatum est illi ad justitiam: id est, actus ille credendi fuit Deo acceptus, et per eum Abraham a Deo judicatus est justus, præsertim prout justitia virtus est generalis; sicque credendo, meruit justitiæ incrementum, omniumque virtutum profectum. Oportet scire quod verba ex Genesi nunc introducta, dicta sunt Abrahæ antequam Deus ei præcepit ut sibi filium suum Isaac in holocaustum offerret, imo et antequam ei præceptum circumcisionis donavit. Sed fidei magnitudo, qua tunc Abraham credidit Deo, postmodum est suppleta seu approbata a Deo, ac aliis declarata, per hoc quod filium suum paratus fuit offerre, et circa hoc multa exercuit. Unde Deus tunc dixit ad eum: Nunc cognovi, id est, per hæc opera tua alios cognoscere faciam, quod timeas Deum. Et amicus Dei appellatus est Abraham: non in Genesi, sed in Isaia, ubi legitur Deus dixisse, Semen Abraham amici mei.
paras.en: [[2:23|And the scripture was fulfilled|Et suppleta]], that is, verified and plainly proved to others, the Scripture of Genesis, [[2:23|saying|dicens]]: [[2:23|Abraham believed God|Credidit Abraham Deo]] [the margin gives Gen 15:6] when he said to him: [[Gen 15:5|Look up to heaven and number the stars if thou canst|Suspice cælum, et numera stellas ejus, si potes]]: [[Gen 15:5|So shall thy seed be|sic erit semen tuum]]; [[2:23|and it was reputed to him to justice|et reputatum est illi ad justitiam]]: that is, that act of believing was acceptable to God, and through it Abraham was judged just by God, especially as justice is a general virtue [that is, justice taken as the sum of all virtue, not the particular virtue of giving each his due]; and so by believing he merited an increase of justice and progress in all the virtues. It should be known that the words now brought in from Genesis were said to Abraham before God commanded him to offer his son Isaac to him as a holocaust, nay, even before he gave him the commandment of circumcision. But the greatness of the faith with which Abraham then believed God was afterwards fulfilled, or approved by God and declared to others, by this, that he was ready to offer his son, and did many things concerning it. Hence God then said to him: [[Gen 22:12|now I know|Nunc cognovi]], that is, by these works of thine I will make others know, [[Gen 22:12|that thou fearest God|quod timeas Deum]]. [[2:23|and he was called the friend of God|Et amicus Dei appellatus est]], Abraham: not in Genesis but in Isaias, where God is read to have said: [[Is 41:8|the seed of Abraham my friend|Semen Abraham amici mei]] [the margin's verse number could not be read; the words are Is 41:8].

paras.t: In libro Judith quoque legitur: Abraham per multas tribulationes probatus, amicus Dei effectus est. Meruit ergo amicus Dei esse et appellari, Deo in tam arduis consentiendo, atque promptissime obediendo, adversa quoque patientissime tolerando. Nempe in Isaac immolatione resplenduit magna perfectio Abrahæ in fide et obedientia: in fide, quia unicum filium suum ex Sara conjuge sua, paratus fuit offerre, quum tamen ei Deus jam ante promiserit quod ex Isaac nasceretur ei semen electum et innumerabilis populus. Credidit enim Abraham quod Deus posset filium immolatum suscitare a mortuis, ut Apostolus dicit. In eodem quoque resplenduit obedientia maxima, quod carissimum filium promptissimus fuit offerre, propria manu occidere, et occisum incendere, quum tamen hoc esset opus insolitum, durum et nusquam auditum.
paras.en: In the book of Judith too we read: [[Jdt 8:22|Abraham|Abraham]], [[Jdt 8:22|being proved by many tribulations, was made the friend of God|per multas tribulationes probatus, amicus Dei effectus est]]. He merited, then, to be and to be called the friend of God by consenting to God in things so hard, obeying most promptly, and also bearing adversities most patiently. For in the immolation of Isaac the great perfection of Abraham in faith and obedience shone forth: in faith, because he was ready to offer his only son by Sara his wife, though God had already promised him that from Isaac a chosen seed and a numberless people would be born to him[[Gen 17:16||]]. For Abraham believed that God could raise his sacrificed son from the dead, as the Apostle says[[Heb 11:19||]]. In the same deed there shone forth too the greatest obedience, in that he was most prompt to offer his dearest son, to kill him with his own hand, and to burn him when killed, though this was a deed unwonted, hard, and never heard of.

paras.t: Sed prædictis obviare videntur multa quæ ad Romanos scribit Apostolus: Arbitramur, inquiens, hominem sine operibus justificari; et rursus, Si Abraham ex operibus legis justificatus est, habet gloriam, sed non apud Deum. Et prolixe probat ibi Apostolus, quod fides reputata est Abrahæ ad justitiam, non opera. Unde ait ibidem Apostolus: Ex operibus legis non justificabitur omnis caro. Idem etiam ad Galatas docet Apostolus, inter cetera dicens: Qui ex fide sunt, benedicentur cum fideli Abraham: justus enim ex fide vivit. Sed et in Actibus legitur: Fide purificans Deus corda eorum. — Ad ista est duplex responsio: Prima, quod Paulus apostolus vult probare opera præceptorum cærimonialium legis, non esse necessaria ad salutem, quoniam sine eis Abraham placuit Deo, etiam nondum circumcisus. Jacobus vero hic loquitur de operibus præceptorum moralium, quæ in utraque lege jubentur; de his item operibus quæ a Deo alicui specialiter injunguntur, quale fuit quod Abrahæ jussit Isaac immolare. Secunda responsio est, quod apostolus Paulus probare intendit, nulla opera legis alicui ad salutem suffecisse, sine explicita vel implicita fide Christi, qui omnium electorum caput est et salvator. Idcirco fides de ejus adventu, ab exordio necessaria fuit.
paras.en: But many things that the Apostle writes to the Romans seem to stand against what has been said: [[Rom 3:28|we account|Arbitramur]], says he, [[Rom 3:28|a man to be justified|hominem sine operibus justificari]] without works [Denis's shortened wording; the Apostle has "by faith, without the works of the law"]; and again, [[Rom 4:2|if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory, but not before God|Si Abraham ex operibus legis justificatus est, habet gloriam, sed non apud Deum]] [Denis adds *legis*, "of the law"]. And there the Apostle proves at length that it was faith that was reputed to Abraham unto justice, not works. Hence the Apostle says in the same place: [[Rom 3:20|by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified|Ex operibus legis non justificabitur omnis caro]]. The Apostle teaches the same to the Galatians too, saying among other things: [[Gal 3:9|they that are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham|Qui ex fide sunt, benedicentur cum fideli Abraham]]: for [[Gal 3:11|the just man liveth by faith|justus enim ex fide vivit]]. And in the Acts too we read: God [[Acts 15:9|purifying their hearts by faith|Fide purificans Deus corda eorum]]. — To these there is a twofold answer. The first, that the apostle Paul means to prove that the works of the ceremonial precepts of the law are not necessary to salvation, since without them Abraham pleased God, while not yet circumcised. But James speaks here of the works of the moral precepts, which are commanded in both laws; and likewise of those works that are specially enjoined on someone by God, such as was his command to Abraham to sacrifice Isaac. The second answer is that the apostle Paul intends to prove that no works of the law sufficed anyone for salvation without explicit or implicit faith in Christ, who is the head and saviour of all the elect. Therefore faith in his coming was necessary from the beginning.

paras.t: Hinc Jacobus infert: Videtis oculo interiori ex probatis, quoniam ex operibus justificatur homo, et non ex fide tantum: utrumque enim est necessarium ad salutem, imo potissime caritas, sine qua nec fides, nec operatio quæcumque potest esse meritoria ac Deo accepta. Denique dupliciter dicitur aliquis justificari: Primo, per hoc quod a vitiis expurgatur, et gratiam recipit ac virtutes: quod non fit directe et proprie per opera, quum ante caritatis et gratiæ infusionem, nulla sit meritoria actio, aut quæ gratiam mereatur de condigno. Ad hanc tamen justificationem opera bona ex genere, suo modo disponunt et aptant de congruo, dum quod in se est efficit homo. Sic enim et attritio ad contritionem disponere perhibetur. Secundo, dicitur homo justificari, opera justa, virtuosa ac meritoria exercendo, atque in gratia, donis, virtutibusque crescendo. Et ita nunc loquitur sanctus apostolus Jacobus.
